entreat

en-TREET · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To entreat is to beg or plead earnestly.

The villagers entreated the king to lower the grain tax before winter.

Worked Example

With the storm closing in, the climber entreated her partner to turn back while the trail markers were still easy to spot.

She didn't just suggest turning back -- she pleaded earnestly, with urgency and real emotion. That heartfelt begging is what it means to entreat.

How entreat sits among its neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

implore

implore: to beg desperately

beseech

beseech: to plead urgently, in a formal or literary way

Antonyms

demand

demand: to insist forcefully, as if owed

command

command: to give an order with authority

How Strong Is It? — ask → entreat → implore

ask vs. entreat

ask vs. entreat: Asking is plain and everyday -- entreating adds earnest emotion, as if the answer truly matters to your heart.

implore vs. entreat

implore vs. entreat: To implore is even more desperate than to entreat -- closer to begging on your knees.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — en-

prefix — en-: in; to bring into (Old French, from Latin)

root — treat-

root — treat-: to handle, deal with (from tractare) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: En- ('in') + treat- ('to handle, deal with'): to entreat someone began as 'to deal with, to negotiate with' -- and narrowed over time into pleading earnestly with them.

Use the root in a new word: treaty

Use the root in a new word: treaty: The two nations signed a peace treaty after months of careful negotiation.

Root Check

Word Choice

Entreat is earnest and a little formal or literary -- characters in novels entreat; friends usually just ask or beg. It often takes the pattern 'entreat someone to do something.'
